meta_desc: Grade 1 addition worksheet guide in the right order: within 10, within 20, number bonds, adding 3 numbers and word problems. Free quiz and printable PDF.
excerpt: Most Grade 1 addition worksheets are handed out in the wrong order, so children hit carrying sums before their number bonds are solid. Here is the practice sequence I use, chapter by chapter, with a free quiz to check where your child actually is.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is the mistake I see in half the Grade 1 workbooks parents show me: the very first page has sums like 8 + 7 and 9 + 6, questions that cross ten, sitting right next to a child who still counts 3 + 2 on her fingers. The child stalls, the parent worries, and everyone decides maths is ‘hard’. It is not hard. The worksheet was just in the wrong order.

A good maths worksheet for Grade 1 addition is not one big pile of sums. It is a staircase. Each step should be nearly automatic before the next one arrives. Below is the exact order I hand practice out in — the same order the NCERT-aligned Maths-Magic Grade 1 book roughly follows — so you can look at any worksheet and know whether it is the right one for your child today.

The Grade 1 addition staircase, step by step

Six things get practised over the year, and they build on each other. Skip a step and the next one collapses.

  • Adding within 10 — sums whose answer is 10 or less (4 + 3, 6 + 2). This is where counting-on is learned.
  • Number bonds to 10 — the pairs 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5. Not sums to solve, but pairs to know.
  • Adding within 20 — crossing ten (8 + 5, 7 + 6), which needs the bonds above.
  • Adding three numbers — 3 + 4 + 2, where the child learns to look for a friendly pair first.
  • Missing-number sums — 6 + __ = 9, which quietly introduces subtraction and algebra thinking.
  • Word problems — short stories where the child has to decide that this is an add.

Step 1 and 2: within 10, then bonds

Worksheets here should be gentle: horizontal sums, plenty of picture support (five apples plus three apples), and answers no bigger than ten. The single most valuable page in the whole year is a number-bonds-to-ten worksheet — ‘how many more to make 10?’ done until the answers come without a pause. In my experience teaching six-year-olds, a fortnight spent here saves two months of struggle later. If your child hesitates on 6 + __ = 10, do not move on. That gap will reappear on every carrying sum.

Step 3: crossing ten (adding within 20)

This is the step most home practice rushes. Adding 8 + 5 is not counting eight fingers and then five more — that is exactly the finger-counting we want to retire. It is making ten: take 2 from the 5 to fill the 8 up to 10, then add the leftover 3 to get 13. A worksheet at this stage should show the ten-frame or the split, not just the bare sum, until the method is habit.

How to spot a worksheet that is too hard

If your child gets more than two or three wrong on a within-20 page and is going back to fingers each time, the bonds from Step 2 are not solid yet. Drop back a step for a few days. Nobody ‘fails’ addition; they just met a page too early.

Step 4 and 5: three numbers and missing numbers

Adding three numbers is where a small idea pays off for years: you can add in any order. For 7 + 2 + 3, a clever child spots that 7 + 3 makes ten first, then adds the 2. Worksheets should mix in a few of these ‘find the friendly pair’ sums rather than always going left to right. Missing-number sums (4 + __ = 9) look small but do a big job — they turn addition around and plant the seed of subtraction without ever using the word.

Step 6: word problems

The last step is stories: ‘Rahul has 6 marbles and Aisha gives him 5 more.’ The maths is easy by now; the skill is reading the situation and deciding it is an add. Keep the numbers small and the sentences shorter than you think they need to be. One honest caveat: read the first few problems aloud together. At six, a reading wall can look exactly like a maths wall, and confusing the two is the fastest way to dent a child’s confidence.

How much practice, and in what order

StepWorksheet typeExampleReady for next when…
1Adding within 106 + 3counts on from the bigger number

4Adding 3 numbers7 + 2 + 3hunts for a pair that makes ten

Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday, every time. One sheet, marked together, with the two or three misses talked through — that is a good day. The weekend is for a mixed page where the child has to choose which method fits, because choosing is where real fluency shows.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Addition Worksheet Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions that climb the Grade 1 addition staircase, from adding within 10 to a word problem. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 1 addition practice, within 10 and within 20

questions.explanation: Start from the bigger number, 5, and count on four: 6, 7, 8, 9.
The bonds to ten include 4 and 6, so 4 + 6 = 10.
Make ten: take 2 from the 5 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: Which is the smart first step for 7 + 2 + 3?
questions.explanation: 7 and 3 make ten, so add them first, then add the 2 to get 12. Order does not matter in addition.
Count on from 6 to 9: 7, 8, 9 is three steps, so the missing number is 3.
Make ten: take 1 from the 6 to turn 9 into 10, then add the leftover 5. 10 + 5 = 15.

questions.q: Rahul has 6 marbles and Aisha gives him 5 more. How many now?
questions.explanation: This is an add: 6 + 5. Make ten by moving 4 from the 5, then add 1 more. The answer is 11.
Add in any order. 3 + 2 makes 5, then 5 + 4 = 9.

faq.q: What should a Grade 1 addition worksheet start with?
faq.a: Sums within 10 with picture support, then number bonds to ten. Bare sums that cross ten (like 8 + 7) come later — putting them on the first page is the most common reason a child stalls.

faq.q: In what order should addition topics be practised in Grade 1?
faq.a: Within 10, then bonds to ten, then within 20 (crossing ten), then adding three numbers, then missing-number sums, and finally word problems. Each step relies on the one before it.

faq.q: How do I know a worksheet is too hard for my child?
faq.a: If they get more than two or three wrong on a page and keep going back to finger-counting, the earlier step is not secure. Drop back one step for a few days rather than pushing on.

faq.q: How much addition practice a day is right at this age?
faq.a: About ten focused minutes — one short worksheet marked together, with the misses talked through. Daily and small beats a long weekly session for six- and seven-year-olds.
